description: We are four engineering majors participating in the "Be an Earth System Trend Detective." We're going to be building a tool where you pick a variable and a region, plot the time series, and test whether the trend is statistically significant. Our team is full, and we're locked in on the coding, signal processing, and statistics. We bring good vibes and bad puns. Wish us Luck!!
summary:
AI data centers are being built faster than communities can study what they do to the land around them. A single facility can use millions of gallons of water, heat the surrounding ground, and add air pollution from backup generators, and those effects land on local biomes that are already under stress. Because this build out is not going to stop, we built a web app that lets anyone see the likely environmental effects of a data center before it is built.

Now click any point in California or enter coordinates, and Site Atlas returns a 0 to 100 sustainability score from 45 years of NASA data from 1981 to 2025, including ground heat, summer highs, soil moisture, and rainfall. Our "Can We Build Datacenters Here?" tool then simulates placing a data center at that spot and shows how soil moisture, temperature, evapotranspiration, air quality, and vegetation would change, ending in a clear verdict and an engineering recommendation. Hence, our Site Atlas web app helps builders choose lower impact sites and gives communities facts instead of guesses.
details:
AI data centers are being built faster than communities can study their effects. One data center in Iowa used about 1 billion gallons of water in 2024, enough to supply all of the state's homes for five days, and a proposed site near Quantico Creek in Virginia was projected to send roughly 95 large dump trucks of sediment into the creek. Because this build out will not stop, the real question is where data centers should go. Our team, The Unemployables, built a fully interactive, accurate trained AI model web app to answer that with NASA data.

Site Atlas is our interactive web app for California and its nine biomes. A user simply clicks a point on the map or enters coordinates, and the app identifies the biome and loads NASA data for that location, including ground heat, summer highs, soil moisture, and rainfall from 1981 to 2025. It returns a 0 to 100 suitability score built from summer coolness, water supply, underground moisture, and heatwave safety. The "Can We Any Datacenters Build Here?" tool then simulates placing a data center there and measures how soil moisture, temperature, evapotranspiration, air quality, and vegetation would change. It combines them into one weighted score, with 0 to 40 suitable, 41 to 60 suitable with conditions, and 61 to 100 avoid. It ends with a plain language verdict and an engineering recommendation, such as zero water closed loop cooling and clean backup power.

To build it, we sampled points across California, gathered NASA hydrology and climate variables, and found that seasonal averages describe the data far better than yearly averages. We used a PCA to identify the most important variables and trained an AI model to classify biomes, which lets us estimate how a facility would shift conditions at each site. The site is built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet.js, and OpenStreetMap.

Site Atlas helps builders choose lower impact sites, gives communities clear facts, and shows NASA which metrics could track data center impacts, including what a data center-focused satellite should measure. It is a screening tool that supports, and does not replace, formal environmental review. With more time, we would add more variables and expand from California to the whole country and then the world.

Claude, Gemini 4 Argon, and Antigravity were used to help build the coordinate entry map interface and brainstorm and draft this write up.
